name: White tie dressing

lead: White tie is the most formal evening dress code. Men wear a black tailcoat, white piqué waistcoat and bow tie, a wing-collar shirt and black trousers with silk stripes, finished with patent court shoes. The tailored cut, high waist and strong black-and-white contrast create a long, V-shaped formal silhouette.
It is now rare and mostly appears at state banquets, royal events, balls and galas such as the Nobel Banquet and Vienna Opera Ball.

paras: People rent or buy the components, usually have the tailcoat and trousers fitted so the waistcoat does not show below the coat front, and add optional items such as gloves, top hat and boutonniere. Women wear full-length gowns.

The main drawbacks are cost, rarity and strict etiquette: wearing it where black tie is expected, or the wrong colours, can look out of place. Rules differ slightly between authorities such as Debrett's and tailors.

angle.text: The tailored coat, high waist and white-on-black contrast give a formal, elongated look worn to the most formal evening occasions.

lead: White tie, also called full evening dress or a dress suit, is the most formal Western evening dress code.[1] For men it consists of a black cutaway tailcoat with silk-faced lapels, a white piqué waistcoat, a starched wing-collar shirt, a white bow tie, black high-waisted trousers with two silk stripes, and patent leather court shoes.[1]

For looks, the cut elongates the leg line and emphasises the chest and shoulders; wearers rely on tailoring, and the code limits colours to black and white. Women wear a full-length ball gown, gloves and optionally a tiara.[1]
The code emerged from late 18th-century dark dress coats, settled by the 1870s, and became distinct from black tie in the early 20th century.[1]

paras: Men: black tailcoat, white piqué low-cut waistcoat, white wing-collar shirt with starched or piqué bib, white bow tie, black trousers with galon stripes, patent court shoes. Optional accessories include top hat, white gloves, white scarf, pocket watch, boutonniere, and miniature orders and medals.[1]

Austere dark dress coats became fashionable in the late 18th century, and Beau Brummell's minimalism helped establish black and white for evening by the 1840s.[1] The dinner jacket appeared in the 1880s as a more comfortable alternative, and white tie then became distinct from black tie.[1] It declined after World War I, revived in the 1930s, and John F. Kennedy was the last US president to wear it at an inauguration, in 1961.[1]

It is worn in the evening for state and royal events, the Nobel Banquet, the Vienna Opera Ball, university balls, doctoral conferments, Mardi Gras balls and occasionally the Met Gala.[1] Only black and white are used, and the waistcoat should not show below the tailcoat front.[1] Tailors consider single linked cuffs more traditional, while Debrett's accepts double cuffs.[1]

timeline.event: Black and white become standard evening colours.[1]
The dinner jacket emerges as a more comfortable alternative.[1]
JFK is the last US president to wear white tie at an inauguration.[1]
